solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Repeatedly attack crowd backing poet (7)

indicators.note: going backwards, so MOB is read right to left

annotation.surface: A mob keeps turning on a poet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like the crowd supporting the poet; it actually turns MOB back to front.
annotation.definitionFit: To bombard is to attack again and again, with shells or with questions.

entries.clue: Feel unhappy about pulse, getting doctor in (6)

indicators.note: the pulse gets something put into it
'in' as in 'getting a doctor in': MO is called into the middle of BEAN

blocks.note: a bean is a pulse, an edible seed

annotation.surface: Someone is anxious about their pulse and calls in a doctor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' reads as a heartbeat next to 'doctor'; here it is the vegetable, BEAN.
annotation.definitionFit: To bemoan something is to feel or express unhappiness about it.

entries.clue: Critic of behaviour is rupturing self-confidence, right? (9)

indicators.note: IS bursts into MORALE, splitting it

annotation.surface: A censorious critic damages someone's self-esteem, and asks if that is fair.
annotation.walkthrough: IS breaks MORALE into MORAL…E, and R is tacked on the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A moraliser passes judgement on how other people behave.

entries.clue: Vocally register supporting Anna Freud, for one (7)

indicators.note: spoken out loud, so the sound counts, not the spelling
in a down clue, LIST sits under ANNA and holds her up

annotation.surface: A note about the psychoanalyst Anna Freud, perhaps her singing voice.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'Anna Freud' as one name, but the definition is only 'Freud, for one' — Sigmund or Anna, both were psychoanalysts.
annotation.definitionFit: Freud is the classic example of a psychoanalyst, commonly shortened to analyst.

entries.clue: Trouble, having soiled big pants (9)

indicators.note: British slang for rubbish, so the letters are made a mess of

annotation.surface: An embarrassing accident with some large underwear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like a noun, the underwear; it is the British adjective meaning rubbish, telling you to jumble the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to disoblige is to put someone out, to cause them bother.

entries.clue: I’d say competently performs work one has to face (4,3)

indicators.note: the setter speaking, so what follows is heard rather than read

blocks.note: someone who does it well knows the job
the setter's 'I'd say' marks the whole phrase as speech, heard not spelt

annotation.surface: A remark about a skilled worker who faces up to their job.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Work' does double duty: it gives JOB, and the definition leans on it — a job one has done to one's face, not a task one must confront.
annotation.definitionFit: Cosmetic surgery on the nose is work carried out on the face, so the definition reads as 'a job one has to the face'.

entries.clue: Dinner, vegetarian, including bottle (5)

indicators.note: the first words include the answer within them

annotation.surface: A menu note: vegetarian dinner, bottle of wine included.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' is British slang for courage, not a wine bottle.
annotation.definitionFit: Bottle and nerve both mean courage.

entries.clue: Obnoxious individual finally breaks fiddle (7)

indicators.note: take the final letter of the next word

blocks.note: to tinker is to fiddle with something

annotation.surface: A nasty person ends up smashing a violin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' suggests the violin, but it is the verb, to tinker.
annotation.definitionFit: A stinker is a thoroughly unpleasant person.

entries.clue: Obscure man receiving good justice (5)

indicators.note: to receive is to take in, so JUDE takes G into his middle

blocks.note: Jude the Obscure, Thomas Hardy's novel

annotation.surface: An unknown fellow gets fair treatment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' reads as a verb or adjective; it names Hardy's hero, Jude the Obscure.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Justice' is the formal title of a High Court judge, as in Mr Justice Smith, so the word names the office.

entries.clue: Servant stabs live mouse (5,3)

indicators.note: LACKEY pierces BE, ending up inside it

annotation.surface: A servant kills a mouse.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mouse' is slang for a bruised eye, not the rodent.
annotation.definitionFit: A mouse is slang for a black eye, from its swollen, dark look.

entries.clue: Duck giving answer in combination (9)

indicators.note: 'in' places ANS within MERGER, splitting it MERG…ER

annotation.surface: Someone ducks a question by giving a combined answer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Duck' reads as a verb, to dodge; it is the bird.
annotation.definitionFit: A merganser is a fish-eating diving duck.

entries.clue: At length, I land (5)

blocks.note: the letter I spelt out in full in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Someone finally makes landfall after a long voyage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At length' reads as 'eventually'; it means written out at full length: I is INDIA in the radio alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: India is the code word for I, and also a country.

entries.clue: Narrow lane heading off from depressed region (5)

indicators.note: the head, the first letter, comes off

blocks.note: VALLEY, a low-lying region, loses its V

annotation.surface: A narrow lane leads away from a poor district.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Depressed region' suggests an economic slump; it is a valley, physically lower.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a lane squeezed between buildings is exactly what an alley is.

entries.clue: Very quick drink after interval (9)

indicators.note: 'after' is literal order: the drink word is written after the interval word

blocks.note: to neck is British slang for gulping a drink

annotation.surface: Someone downs a drink fast at the interval.
annotation.walkthrough: To neck a drink is British slang for gulping it down.
annotation.definitionFit: Breakneck speed is dangerously fast.

entries.clue: Two characteristics of attractive model in easy circumstances (7,6)

annotation.surface: Describing an artist's model who has an easy life.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay describes one model twice: she is sitting (for a painter) and she is pretty.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone comfortably off, with no worries, is said to be sitting pretty.

entries.clue: Career politician leads area that won’t be developed (5,4)

indicators.note: GREEN goes in front of BELT

blocks.note: a member of the Green Party
to career is to rush along, to belt

annotation.surface: An ambitious professional politician leads a local planning argument.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Career politician' is a stock phrase, but the words split: 'career' is the verb, to belt along.
annotation.definitionFit: A green belt is protected land around a town where building is restricted.

entries.clue: Churning out orders for royal badge (5,4)

indicators.note: stirring the letters about

annotation.surface: A factory mass-producing orders for royal insignia.
annotation.walkthrough: The Tudor rose is the red-and-white rose emblem of the Tudor dynasty.
annotation.definitionFit: The Tudor rose is the heraldic badge of England's royal house.

entries.clue: Ruffle cat’s coat, bare at the sides and coarse (8)

indicators.note: only the letters at each edge of BARE

annotation.surface: Someone strokes a cat the wrong way; its coat is patchy at the flanks and rough.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ruffle' looks like a verb about stroking fur; it is the noun, a frill on a dress.
annotation.definitionFit: A dressmaking term: a furbelow is a pleated frill sewn on a skirt, the noun sense of ruffle.

entries.clue: Without help in court here, endure being cast outside (13)

indicators.note: to cast metal is to pour it into a new form, so ENDURE's letters are remoulded
the jumbled letters sit around PRESENT

annotation.surface: A defendant without a lawyer must put up with being thrown out.
annotation.walkthrough: PRESENT sits inside the rearranged ENDURE.
annotation.definitionFit: A litigant with no lawyer acting for them is unrepresented.

entries.clue: Prepare to pass magazine insert (4,3)

blocks.note: a driver pulls out before overtaking

annotation.surface: Getting ready to hand over a magazine supplement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pass' means overtake on the road, not hand over.
annotation.definitionFit: You pull out to overtake, and a pull-out is a removable section of a magazine.

entries.clue: Primate cheers cardinal suppressing resistance (7)

indicators.note: MAIN holds R down inside it

annotation.surface: A top churchman silences a rebellion while a primate applauds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Primate' and 'cardinal' both suggest churchmen; 'primate' is the monkey and 'cardinal' means main.
annotation.definitionFit: A tamarin is a small South American monkey.

entries.clue: Here perhaps film the sort of poker I love (6)

blocks.note: stud is a form of poker

annotation.surface: Someone suggests filming a poker game here.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition reads 'a place where you might film': a studio.
annotation.definitionFit: Films are often shot in a studio.

entries.clue: Outlaw stealing quartz of large church (9)

indicators.note: BAN takes SILICA and holds it inside

blocks.note: quartz is a form of silica

annotation.surface: A bandit steals crystal from a cathedral.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw' reads as a bandit; it is the verb, to ban.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective from the Roman building type: a basilica is a large oblong church, and basilican describes things belonging to one.

entries.clue: Millions living in a certain area of France (5)

indicators.note: something living in a house is inside it, so M is housed inside SOME

blocks.note: some = a certain, as in 'some person'

annotation.surface: A population count for a French region.
annotation.walkthrough: The Somme is a department of northern France, famous for the First World War battle.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Somme is one of France's administrative departments, named after its river.

entries.clue: Threw away European social position (5)

annotation.surface: A European gave up their social standing.
annotation.walkthrough: CAST followed by E.
annotation.definitionFit: Caste is a fixed rank in a social hierarchy.

entries.clue: Revolutionary stabbed in centre of Bath, hurt beforehand (5)

indicators.note: the middle two letters of BATH
'beforehand' means earlier, so the hurt word comes first in the answer

annotation.surface: The murder of Jean-Paul Marat, stabbed in his bath.
annotation.walkthrough: Marat, a leader of the French Revolution, was stabbed in his bath by Charlotte Corday; the capital B makes the bath look like the English city.
annotation.definitionFit: Marat was the French revolutionary famously killed in his bath.

entries.clue: Leg over? Everything under, doing this (5)

annotation.surface: Instructions for a dance: leg this way, everything under.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition describes the limbo dance, where everything must pass under the bar; 'Leg over' is also a cheeky British idiom for sex.
annotation.definitionFit: In limbo dancing the whole body goes under a low bar.

entries.clue: A couple of promises one can’t politely come out with (9)

annotation.definition: one can’t politely come out with

blocks.note: giving your word is a promise

annotation.surface: Two pledges that are too rude to say out loud.
annotation.walkthrough: SWEAR and WORD are each a kind of promise, and together they are what polite people avoid saying.
annotation.definitionFit: A swear word is one you can't use in polite company.

entries.clue: With change of heart, English become twisted (7)

indicators.note: the letters of HEART are changed around

annotation.surface: An Englishman changes his mind and becomes bitter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Change of heart' looks like a change to the middle letter of something; here the word HEART itself is rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: To wreathe is to twist or coil around.

entries.clue: Behind time, duke’s deputy is cross (7)

indicators.note: 'behind' means following on, so ANGELO is written after T

blocks.note: Angelo is the Duke's deputy in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure

annotation.surface: A duke's stand-in is angry at arriving late.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry; it is a hybrid, the tangerine–pomelo cross.
annotation.definitionFit: A tangelo is a citrus cross between a tangerine and a pomelo or grapefruit.
